title: What Happened with “Valley of the Moms”? Unpacking the North Shore Book Feud

content: Photo by Nina Gallant By late June , Alexandra was looking for another audiobook to listen to in the car. She’d selected author Hannah Selinger’s summer fiction debut, Valley of the Moms , largely because the novel was set in her hometown of Hamilton, Massachusetts. The suburban thriller, though outside of Alexandra’s typical genre, seemed interesting enough. Inspired by Selinger’s highly publicized dispute with the Boxford Parent Teacher Organization in 2023, the story centers on Anna, a fictional mother of two who challenges the exclusionary practices of Hamilton’s all-powerful PTO president before turning up dead in the Ipswich River. Alexandra listened to the audiobook shortly after its release and was not impressed. When she finished, she posted a review on Audible. “Other than the lovely narration, this book was painful to get through,” she wrote, noting that it felt slow and predictable. Then she moved on to her next book. The author, however, did not. On June 30, Alexandra’s phone started pinging. Friends were sending her screenshots of Instagram Stories posted by Selinger, which I have reviewed. Not only was Alexandra’s full name repeated there, but her hometown and occupation were also disclosed. Several other local women were listed, too. In the posts, Selinger accused Alexandra and the other women of “review bombing” Valley of the Moms —coordinating one-star reviews on Goodreads and other platforms to drive down the book’s rating. She accused them of stalking. She also claimed Alexandra and several of the other women she named had attended her June 23 author event at the Book Shop of Beverly Farms to publicly attack both her and her book. Alexandra says she hadn’t coordinated her review with anyone. But one accusation wasn’t merely false. It was impossible. “My 11-year-old daughter had brain surgery the day before that event,” she said. “I was at her bedside. So no, I was not at [Selinger’s] book event.” The irony was difficult to miss. Valley of the Moms is, at its core, a story about what happens when an ordinary suburban dispute catches fire. Within weeks of publication, the novel was at the center of one of its own. I wasn’t really expecting the blowback from anyone besides Boxford, to be honest,” Hannah Selinger said. Like thousands of others , I first encountered the chatter around Valley of the Moms through Instagram. An algorithm delivered a video Selinger posted after her June 23 appearance at the Book Shop of Beverly Farms. In it, she described how a routine author event had gone off the rails: Three women, one of whom Selinger said had identified herself as a former president of Hamilton’s parent-teacher organization (called the Friends of Winthrop), had challenged her publicly during the discussion. The women accused the novel of denigrating women, portraying Hamilton unfairly, and implying corruption within the Hamilton Police Department. (I was unable to identify the woman who Selinger said had presented herself as the former PTO president, or either of the other two women at the event.) “You could hear in [one of the women’s voices] that she was very emotionally charged,” said Namrata Patel, a Boston-based women’s fiction author who moderated Selinger’s event that evening and witnessed the altercation. “She took offense to the book, and that’s what she shared with us and the broader audience. The two other women were also really becoming more antagonistic about how this is not a representation of the town.” Eventually, the exchange became tense enough that staffers asked the women to leave, and the trio was escorted out. The audience applauded. The spectacle was almost perfectly meta: An author of a novel about suburban women behaving badly was interrupted by women objecting to the way suburban women were portrayed. Selinger’s social media video recounting the event sparked discussion across social media, including on Instagram and Threads. Commenters compared the confrontation to The Real Housewives . Others joked that this was exactly why they never volunteered for their children’s schools. When I spoke with Selinger by video call the following week, on June 30, she said she was surprised by the attention. “I wasn’t really expecting the blowback from anyone besides Boxford, to be honest,” she said. After all, Valley of the Moms had grown directly out of Selinger’s own experience when she moved from New York back to Massachusetts several years earlier. Shortly after relocating, she attempted to register her son for a Boxford PTO-sponsored family dance called “Ziti with Your Sweetie.” “It was full immediately, like the way Ticketmaster tickets sell out,” she recalled. Through what she described as a “really minor amount of investigative reporting,” Selinger said she learned the local PTO offered families who paid for an annual premium membership early access to event tickets. To her, the issue extended well beyond one sold-out dance. “It’s a public school,” she said. “I didn’t really understand why the dance wasn’t just housed in a larger venue that could accommodate all of the students instead of making it so that indigent families were automatically left out of being able to participate at all.” Selinger sent an email to the PTO bemoaning the timing of a 5 p.m. ticket release as inconvenient for working parents. In response, the PTO offered a waitlist and a telephone discussion with a board member. Selinger then replied, her lawyer says, with an email addressing “unequal access and the exclusion of children” and “alerting the PTO of her intent to go to the media with her concerns.” Selinger emailed the PTO again two days later before going to the local news stations. Jackie, a Boxford PTO board member at the time, who asked me not to use her real name, said despite the email exchange, Selinger never took the organization up on its offer to discuss the issue by phone before going public. That experience became the catalyst for Selinger’s novel. “I wanted to sort of discuss wealth and class and modern parenting through the prism of this PTO,” she said. Her literary agent, however, advised against placing the story in Boxford itself. “He was like, ‘Don’t set it where you send your children to school,’” Selinger recalled. The concern was practical, not literary. Though several years had passed since the dispute, her agent worried publishing a novel set in Boxford would inevitably reignite local tensions. Instead, Selinger relocated the fictional conflict to the town next door, Hamilton. “Hamilton [is] a really sort of comparable one-to-one town,” she said, pointing to its equestrian history, expansive homes, and generational wealth. But the North Shore itself was always intended to be more than a setting. “I felt really strongly about the North Shore as its own character in this book.” To Selinger, the Book Shop of Beverly Farms confrontation was proof that the novel had accurately captured the social dynamics she hoped to explore. “The fact that she didn’t see how meta it was and how much she was just representing all of the tropes that I was leaning into was wild to me,” she said of one of the women who interrupted her event. Explaining why she believed some readers had reacted so intensely, Selinger said the answer was simple. “What are they so upset about if it’s not about them?” she said. “Obviously it is you.… It is a mirror. But you can’t fess up to it, because then you have to admit your own guilt.” While Selinger acknowledged that some Hamilton residents had criticized the novel, she said she believed the backlash reflected a vocal minority rather than widespread community sentiment. She told me she had received supportive messages from many local readers while simultaneously becoming convinced that others were coordinating negative Goodreads reviews and organizing criticism in neighborhood Facebook groups. Then the interview took an unexpected turn. Selinger began reading aloud to me the names of women she believed had posted one-star Goodreads ratings, identifying reviewers she suspected lived in Hamilton. After our interview ended, she sent me the list of names she had offered to share. She also described monitoring online discussions surrounding the novel. Then she mentioned one reviewer whose rating had recently disappeared. “That woman took hers down,” she said. “Because I emailed her work. She deserved it.” Later that night, Selinger went further. Over the course of the evening, she published multiple Instagram Stories naming women she believed were responsible for what she characterized as a review-bombing campaign against Valley of the Moms on Goodreads and other platforms. The posts identified individuals by name, in some cases alongside details including their occupations and other affiliations. They spread rapidly online after Selinger urged her followers to “make them famous!” The debut novel of North Shore author Hannah Selinger (pictured circa 2020), Valley of the Moms, became the center of a dispute over negative online reviews. / Photo by Lindsay Morris/The New York Times/Redux pictures By the early morning , Selinger’s name was a trending topic. Dozens of users criticized her posts, called for them to be removed, and demanded that the author apologize to the women she had identified. Some called on her publisher to publicly condemn what they characterized as harassment of book reviewers. Most of the women Selinger had named declined to speak with me or requested anonymity, citing fears of further retaliation by the author. Several pointed me to a 2015 criminal case involving Selinger and her half-sister. According to the complaint, Selinger was accused of posting her half-sister’s phone number on Instagram alongside language suggesting she was looking for sexual partners, which led to unwanted calls. Selinger was also accused of submitting RSVPs to her half-sister’s wedding under Selinger’s own name, her dog’s name, and her deceased father’s name. Selinger’s lawyer said Selinger denies operating the Instagram account that made the posts in dispute and said that subpoenaed Instagram records during the proceedings showed that the account was a spoof, but he did not provide documentation supporting that claim. He said the charges were later dismissed. The decision to publicly identify reviewers also changed the tenor of the dispute. “When she circulated it to her profile saying, ‘make them famous,’ which kind of crossed the line from just defending her work into targeted harassment, I think that was where people really started to get afraid,” said Tara, a North Shore resident who asked to be identified under a pseudonym out of fear of retaliation by Selinger. Tara read the novel along with several local mom friends, some of whom were called out in Selinger’s posts. Alexandra also asked that her last name not be used in this article. “When people Google me, I don’t want the only thing that comes up is being embroiled in this ridiculous drama,” she said with a laugh. “The author will know it’s me.” She maintains she did exactly what online review sites were designed for: She read a book, formed an opinion, and left a review. Alexandra was stunned by Selinger’s accusations. “I just found it to be extremely bizarre,” she told me. “She publicly accused us of stalking her and going to her event.” To her, it seemed as though Selinger believed any Hamilton resident who left a negative review was trying to tank the book in coordination with other Hamilton residents. After Selinger’s post naming several commenters she believed were review-bombing her book, several women pointed out that one of the people named appeared to be a teenager. (I independently confirmed that one of the names Selinger called out in her posts matches the name of a teenage Hamilton resident. I could identify no other Hamilton residents sharing that name.) “Any amount of digging would have revealed she was not an adult,” Alexandra said. “She is a child.” In response to that allegation, Selinger’s attorney said that Selinger “maintains that she did not know any account she identified belonged to a minor and did not knowingly target a child.” After publication, Selinger’s attorney objected that there is no “verification that the teenager controlled the account.” Selinger’s lawyer said that the author selected “particularly egregious fake reviews and republished the public material on Instagram with the names the reviewers themselves had used.” He noted that Selinger did not “reveal previously private information or direct threats of harassment,” adding that the posts were intended to allow readers to judge the reviewers’ conduct for themselves. The posts I reviewed also included reviewers’ occupations and volunteer associations, with Selinger saying she would contact their employers, though none of the reviewers I contacted said they ultimately faced professional consequences. As criticism of Selinger’s posts mounted online, the author removed them and temporarily made her social media accounts private. In the wake of the online criticism, she asserted that her actions had been “misrepresented” and that she had been the victim of an organized harassment campaign. At presstime, Valley of the Moms was still on Goodreads , with a 2.91 overall rating. Several one-star ratings Selinger complained about had been removed, as had several five-star ratings. But which ratings were removed by Goodreads or by the readers themselves is unclear. Others she called out remained on the site. Hannah Selinger during a panel discussion in 2023, three years before the release of her debut novel. / WBUR NPR Boston By the time I spoke with Selinger again three weeks later, the controversy surrounding her social media posts had eclipsed the author event that first drew attention to the book online. Before we began our on-the-record conversation, she established one condition: She would not discuss her social media posts. Instead, we talked about Goodreads. Selinger maintained that Valley of the Moms had been subjected to a coordinated review-bombing campaign rather than ordinary literary criticism. “Obviously, there’s going to be some people that don’t like my book, and some of them may live in Hamilton,” she told me during our second interview. “But that’s not what was happening here.” She described a small but vocal group organizing in local Facebook communities before flooding Goodreads with one-star ratings. Selinger said her publisher, Little, Brown, had contacted Goodreads to request an investigation; on June 23, according to Selinger’s lawyer, the website responded to an inquiry from Selinger, noting, “We have investigated this situation and taken appropriate action as needed.” On July 22, according to an email provided by Selinger’s lawyer, Goodreads followed up directly with Selinger, saying it had determined that several accounts that gave the book negative reviews were “illegitimate” and had been removed. (When asked to authenticate that message, Goodreads said it was “unable to confirm or deny the authenticity of the communication.”) Selinger’s lawyer also said that Goodreads “temporarily [restricted] activity on the book because it had detected behavior inconsistent with its review guidelines.” Little, Brown, however, offered a narrower account. Asked for a statement, a representative for the company said, “We value our relationship with Goodreads and respect their Ratings & Review and Community Guidelines. On July 4, we received a notification from the Goodreads support team that they investigated reviews of the book and took ‘appropriate action as needed.’ We received no additional details, and Little, Brown took no further action.” When asked for comment about the alleged review-bomb campaign, Goodreads said it does not comment on individual cases, but pointed me to its author guidelines , which explicitly prohibit authors from engaging with users who have left negative ratings or reviews. Asked to define review bombing, a Goodreads representative pointed to its community guidelines, which prohibit “artificially inflating or deflating a book’s ratings or reputation,” including “activity like creating fake accounts to manipulate book ratings, purchasing reviews, and incentivizing votes, likes, or other actions on Goodreads.” Review bombing is not inherently about negativity. Its defining feature is manipulation: artificially changing the perception or reputation of a work, whether by dragging its rating down or pushing it up. And Selinger is far from the first author to find herself immersed in its murky waters. In 2023, Elizabeth Gilbert halted the publication of her novel The Snow Forest after hundreds of negative Goodreads ratings criticized her decision to set the story in Russia amid the war in Ukraine. That same year, debut author Cait Corrain admitted to creating fake Goodreads accounts to artificially boost her own book’s rating while posting negative reviews of fellow debut authors’ books. Her publisher subsequently canceled her book deal. But what actually counts as review bombing? The answer is surprisingly difficult to pin down. Gianluca Stringhini, an associate professor in the department of electrical and computer engineering at Boston University who studies coordinated online behavior, says there is no universally accepted definition—“precisely because it’s kind of a spectrum,” he says. “It can be something like I create a bunch of fake accounts, I press a button, and they post either positive reviews, maybe somebody paid me to boost a business or something like that, or negative reviews if somebody’s paying me to, or if I want to badmouth somebody or trash somebody.” On the other end of the spectrum are “grassroots type of activities where people coordinate to go and post reviews, typically negative reviews, for a business, for a book, or a product,” Stringhini explained. The distinction matters. Platforms like Goodreads generally prohibit automated or inauthentic activity from fake accounts and bots. But when real people use their own accounts to express genuine opinions, regardless of their motivations, the line becomes considerably less clear. “When it comes from real people, and there is some grassroots activity of sorts,” Stringhini says, “that becomes trickier because then there are free-speech issues.” That could be a crucial distinction in the Valley of the Moms controversy. If a group of women from Hamilton got together to read the book, collectively disliked it, and independently posted negative reviews from their own established Goodreads accounts, Stringhini says, “I think that would fall more under legitimate or allowed use.… It’s basically free speech, expressing their opinions.” So how could someone determine whether negative reviews were left by fake accounts or a group of book-club moms? Stringhini emphasized that identifying coordinated or manipulated activity is difficult and that platforms have access to information unavailable to the public. But there are signals he says users can examine when trying to distinguish manufactured activity from genuine reviews. Account history is one clue. Stringhini says a cluster of freshly created accounts with no history posting reviews about the same book or product would be evidence of “manufactured activity.” People can also look for evidence of coordination across platforms, as well as similarities in timing and language. Those criteria raise another question in this case. Selinger publicly called out a number of negative reviews as fraudulent. But the reviews she identified did not share at least one of the characteristics Stringhini identified: The reviewers Selinger named publicly were identifiable people, one of whom I spoke with. I contacted several others, but they declined to speak with me on the record, several citing fear of retaliation based on Selinger’s online behavior. At the same time, roughly half a dozen five-star ratings displayed some of the characteristics Stringhini identified as potential signs of manufactured activity. The accounts had no followers and no apparent review history. One review was dated six months before the book’s release. That review was posted under an account sharing the name of the best-friend character in the novel. Selinger’s lawyer, however, said Selinger had no knowledge of who posted the reviews and denied that she had any connection to them. He also noted that publishers routinely distribute advance copies before publication, allowing legitimate reviews to appear before a book’s release. Whether Selinger was the target of a truly coordinated campaign remains unclear. But a pattern does emerge: When Selinger believed she had been treated unfairly, she had a way of raising the stakes. In Selinger’s own Instagram bio , she describes herself as a “mix of Joris-Karl Huysmans, M.F.K. Fisher, & Regina George”—the latter being the infamous mean girl from the 2004 film Mean Girls . The Goodreads reviewers were not the only people Selinger called out online. In one Instagram Story, she called a woman a “ho.” The woman had given Selinger’s book a one-star review on Amazon, calling it a “POS” and writing that she had heard Selinger was “rude.” Then there was the matter of Alexandra’s 22-year-old son; after he privately messaged Selinger suggesting that the negative reviews she was calling out might simply be because her book wasn’t good, Selinger posted about and identified him on her Instagram Stories using language that directed him to “suck a fatty” and sharing a photo of him. She later accused Alexandra’s son of threatening her. (I reviewed the Instagram direct messages between the two and found no explicit threat in the exchange.) The Goodreads controversy itself has not made its way into a courtroom. But Selinger’s concern for her reputation has previously led her to turn to the courts. In recent years, she has brought civil claims of defamation against at least two North Shore residents over statements made about her online. In November 2025, she sued a Newburyport city councilor alleging defamation, seeking $50,000 in damages for reputational harm after the councilor wrote on Facebook that she had begun locking her doors at night because she believed Selinger posed a threat to her safety and that of other city officials. The case was settled under confidential terms. In a separate case also filed in November 2025, Selinger sued the author of the local newsletter Newburyport Government at a Glance over statements about Selinger’s online behavior. According to court filings, the newsletter alleged that Selinger had a history of harassing several Newburyport city councilors and that she had posted the names of a city councilor’s children and their school affiliation on Instagram. The case is ongoing. Selinger has been on both sides of this. When she believed people had wronged her online, she sometimes identified them publicly. And when she believed other people’s online statements about her crossed a legal line, she sometimes sued. The legal cases don’t establish whether the accusations on either side are true. But they do reveal a tension running through Selinger’s disputes: She has gone to court to defend her own reputation even as she has publicly challenged the reputations of people she believes have wronged her. In an essay she wrote for People magazine , Selinger referred to the drama surrounding her battle with the Boxford PTO as “relatively hilarious.” For the PTO, however, the dispute had lasting effects. Relations between Selinger and the PTO spiraled downward after Selinger went to the media with her complaints about the “Ziti with Your Sweetie” ticketing system. Selinger continued to criticize the organization in media interviews and online, and the dispute cost the PTO money. “She came at the PTO so hardcore that we actually had to hire a lawyer and a PR firm to help us navigate how to move forward,” Jackie, the former Boxford PTO board member, said. “Money that was raised for the schools and giving back, we had to redirect some of those funds.” Meanwhile, the author said she received anonymous harassing messages through the contact form on her website , which she believed came from people associated with the PTO, and she made police reports in 2023. Selinger’s lawyer also said she experienced antisemitic harassment during the dispute. According to an email provided by her lawyer, the matter was brought to the attention of the superintendent of the Tri-Town School Union and the Boxford Police. Jackie said she remains particularly bothered that the ticketing dispute ultimately became the basis for Selinger’s novel. “There is a resentment of her getting to profit personally off our story. If she was going to come back and say the proceeds [from the book] are being donated, that would change. For her to call it fiction and profit from it, but there were real consequences—it doesn’t sit right.” In one of her interviews with the media, Selinger publicly called for a Boxford PTO reelection; at the end of the 2023 school year, the majority of the board resigned. Selinger herself said she had never been inclined to volunteer with the PTO. “I’m a Groucho Marx type. I wouldn’t be a member of any club that would have someone like me as a member,” she said. “I was never going to be in the PTO, even before all of this. I’m not going to be, like, a class mom either.” The episode also made some parents reluctant to get involved. Julie Friedman, the current president of the Boxford PTO, has encountered that reluctance firsthand. “I had a mom this year say, ‘Oh yeah, I was around, you know, a couple years ago when the whole thing with the dance happened. So I would never want to be a part of the PTO. It’s just too much,’” she says. Still, Friedman said the organization is trying to move forward. “Despite all of this, we’re going to continue to treat [Selinger] like a member of the community, treat [her] children like members of the community, invite them in, and be open to conversation with them and feedback,” she said. “And that’s kind of our job. That’s the only thing I really care about: continuing the mission.” For a perspective outside the Boxford dispute, Barbara Gildea has spent eight years with the Kingston Parent Teacher Organization while working full-time in development at a university research institute. “Recruitment has become our top priority,” she said. “Our PTO is a small group of extremely dedicated volunteers, and we’re constantly in the process of recruiting more parents, more families, more guardians to come out…because the more hands that we have, the more we’ll be able to do for the schools.” But on the issue that started it all, Gildea thought Selinger had a point. Membership programs that reward donors with early access or exclusive benefits, she explained, are commonplace in nonprofit organizations like museums, cultural institutions, and research organizations. A PTO, however, occupies a different space. “The mission of the PTO is to improve the school, to support the teachers, to support the kids,” she said. “It’s always something that should benefit everyone.” Offering families preferential access to children’s events in exchange for donations, she believes, runs counter to that mission. “I can also see why,” she said, “people would say applying that model to the PTO is pretty icky.” Selinger, for her part, has maintained that she was targeted first—and continues to be targeted. In June, Valley of the Moms became a USA Today bestseller, drawing even more attention to the story that inspired it. For the people caught in the dispute surrounding it, though, there was no tidy resolution. Selinger, for her part, has maintained that she was targeted first—and continues to be targeted. Her lawyer pointed to recent attempts by individuals to pressure a Melrose bookstore into canceling a September appearance, as well as a police report Selinger filed that month accusing a Boxford official of online harassment. Her lawyer said that her request for a temporary restraining order against the official was not granted. Alexandra’s review, meanwhile, is still up, and she stands by it. Her daughter is recovering well from her surgery. She still enjoys listening to audiobooks, recently giving The Extraordinary Life of Sam Hell five stars and calling it “a masterpiece.” No other authors have commented on her reviews of their work. This story has been updated since publication.
